title: Prioritized streams, kernel binding, and safe graph segmentation for stable multi-stream decode
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: We observe intermittent CUDA graph capture/replay failures and correctness mismatches during concurrent multi-stream decoding when the scheduler switches kernel variants for attention (e.g., fused vs. segmented attention) based on sequence-length histograms. Root causes include: (1) capture paths that assume a fixed kernel variant across prefill+decode, (2) stream priority inversion when background prefill workloads steal resources causing partial captures, and (3) oversized fused kernels that are non-deterministic under certain memory reuse patterns.

Goal: Implement a conservative, observable-safe approach that combines stream prioritization, explicit kernel-to-graph binding, and deterministic graph segmentation to reduce capture instability and replay mismatches while preserving throughput. The solution must allow safe canary rollout and automated fallback to non-graph decode when instability is detected.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Graph segmentation: split capture into two deterministic micro-graphs - a "prefill graph" (bulk KV init) and a small, parameterized "decode step micrograph" (per-token prefix). Segmentation limits the surface area affected by kernel swaps and reduces need for full recapture when only decode kernels change.
2) Kernel binding table: at capture-time, record a compact kernel binding signature (kernel ids, compute capability, chosen attention variant, quantization profile). On replay, validate signature; if mismatch, prefer targeted recapture of the affected micrograph instead of full fallback.
3) Stream priority policy: assign higher priority to latency-sensitive request streams (interactive) and lower to batch prefill streams. Enforce capture preemption rules so a prefill cannot steal a capture window mid-capture. This reduces partial-capture races.
4) Heuristics for capture stability: require observed stability for N consecutive captures before allowing fast-path sticky kernel selection for a given model+seqlen bucket. Expose tunables (N, min_samples) and keep metrics around capture_fail_rate & replay_mismatch_rate.
5) Safe fallback: if decode micrograph replay fails 2x within a minute or if signature mismatch for critical kernels is detected on first replay, route the request to the non-graph decode path and mark the model+bucket unstable. Trigger automated recapture through a background reconciler.
6) Integration with attention optimizations: refuse to merge fused/segmented attention variants into the same graph capture unless the kernel binding signature is stable and unit-tested across the seqlen distribution (test harness described below).

Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (design + tests, 1 sprint): design kernel binding signature format, add capture segmentation APIs to runtime, and build unit tests in the replay harness to inject kernel variant changes.
- Phase 2 (canary, 2 sprints): roll out segmentation + binding to canary nodes in the dev cluster, instrument detailed metrics and a recovery job to perform targeted recapture.
- Phase 3 (gradual rollout, 2-3 sprints): expand to Dedicated pools with traffic weighting and automated rollback triggers based on thresholds.

Observability & metrics: capture_attempts, capture_fail_rate, replay_mismatch_rate, fallback_rate, recapture_count, avg_recapture_latency, kernel_signature_changes. Hook these into the Console per-model dashboard and add alerting thresholds for P0 on regen regressions.

Rollout & safety gates: start with low-traffic models and long tail sequence lengths, require <0.1% replay_mismatch_rate and <0.5% fallback_rate during canary for 48h before expanding. Include one-week kill switch that forces global non-graph routing if regression is detected.

Risks & trade-offs:
- Splitting graphs increases scheduling overhead and may slightly reduce throughput vs monolithic graph capture; acceptable trade for correctness.
- Conservative kernel-binding increases recapture frequency when kernels are updated frequently (e.g., driver or microcode updates). Mitigation: background reconciler and staged updates.
- Complexity in bookkeeping for signature state; requires durable metadata store for per-model bucket signatures.

Open questions:
- How large should the kernel signature be to balance correctness vs storage/latency? (binary fingerprint vs full metadata)
- Should we proactively recapture after driver upgrades or wait for natural recapture triggers?

Artifacts: design doc, unit tests, and canary plan linked below.
